transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-01
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/rec/ff-2026-12-01-rivershore-001 (auto)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Elena Soto (CTO), Tom Briggs (Net Eng), Priya Menon (SecOps), Carlos Ruiz (PM)

Auto-summary (auto gen, rough):
Rivershore is evaluating private deployment options for compliance-bound workloads. Primary concerns: VPC peering vs private endpoints, egress IP control, multi-region data residency, and key management (KMS/HSM). They have a prototype using a hosted LLM endpoint today but need predictable throughput and audit logs. Next steps: share security pack and run a short latency test to validate private endpoint setup.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey, everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE for this account, and we have Ravi and Jordan from our eng team. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Elena Soto: Good, thanks. Busy month but this is high priority for us.
[00:11] Tom Briggs: Hey, yep, morning from my side.
[00:13] Priya Menon: Hi all.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Great. Quick agenda, we'll run through Rivershore's current topology, constraints, then talk options — private endpoints, VPC peering, transit gateway patterns — and call out what Dedicated vs Private deployment would look like. We'll leave time for Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:29] Elena Soto: Yup. We're looking to move inference for PHI workloads off public hosted endpoints. Need either a Private deployment in our VPC or a Dedicated instance with private egress. Security and auditability first, cost and latency also matter.
[00:42] Ravi Patel: Thanks, Elena. Maybe to start Tom, can you sketch out your network today — cloud provider, transit gateway, whether you use AWS RAM peering, that kind of thing?
[00:52] Tom Briggs: Sure. We're mostly in AWS, two prod VPCs in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 for EU data. We use a Transit Gateway in each region and peering between some TGWs for DR. We also have an on-prem colo that talks to the us-east TGW over Direct Connect. CIDRs are overlapping-ish, but we can do non-overlap for the Redwood connector. We currently NAT egress to a fixed IP egress pool for outbound.
[01:17] Maya Chen: Ok, that helps. Quick callout: Redwood Private uses a control plane that can be customer-managed and a data plane that we can bring into your VPC via private endpoints or a peered subnet. There are two common patterns — Private Endpoint (endpoint in your VPC that talks to our service over internal link) or VPC Peering / Transit Gateway where we peer into your VPC and run inferencing there. Each has tradeoffs for egress IP control, cross-region latency, and operational ownership.
[01:48] Priya Menon: On the SOC and keys side, we need KMS integration so keys never leave our account, plus HSM for certain models. Also audit logs, SAML/SSO, and RBAC. We have questions about where logs live and retention.
[01:59] Jordan Lee: For KMS, we can integrate with customer-managed CMKs for Private deployment and our on-prem package supports HSM attachments. Audit logs can be pushed to your cloud logging (we support CloudWatch/Stackdriver) or to a customer SIEM via our forwarder. Retention levels we can configure — what's your retention requirement?
[02:17] Priya Menon: Minimum seven years for certain events.
[02:21] Jordan Lee: Noted, we'll bring our compliance docs.
[02:23] Elena Soto: The tricky part is egress. Our compliance team insists on predictable egress IPs for outbound calls for vendor whitelist. Can Redwood support static egress IPs inside our TGW/NGW?
[02:34] Ravi Patel: Yes. For Private, we can either use your NAT gateways so outbound appears from your egress pool, or we can put an egress NAT under Redwood-managed infra but advertise a static set of IPs that you can whitelist. Tradeoff is who manages the NAT and who owns the IP rotation.
[02:50] Tom Briggs: So if we go with private endpoint, is all traffic fully inside our VPC and uses our NAT? I want to avoid public internet egress.
[02:58] Maya Chen: With private endpoint backed by our data plane inside your VPC, yes traffic stays internal and egress will follow your routing — so your NAT egress IPs are used. There's an option for a carrier-grade egress pool if you prefer Redwood to handle outbound IPs, but that needs contract terms.
[03:17] Priya Menon: We also need to ensure model weights never cross our region for EU data. So if a request originates in eu-west-1, processing must stay in that region. Does Redwood support region pinning?
[03:29] Ravi Patel: We do. We can pin model replicas to regions. For Dedicated, you can select capacity in a given region and pin models. For Private with multi-region presence, we can deploy local workers per region and route by request region. There are nuances — for example, some smaller open models get quantized variants which may have different performance; I'll show performance profiles in the deck.
[03:50] Carlos Ruiz: What's the difference operationally between Dedicated and Private in this context?
[03:54] Maya Chen: Good question. Dedicated is Redwood-managed reserved capacity — guaranteed throughput and a private tenancy pool — but traffic still flows to Redwood's managed network unless you set up a Private Connector. Private is our customer-deployed option where the control plane can be in Redwood but the data plane is inside your VPC or on-prem. Private gives you more control for egress, KMS, and audit log residency, but requires a bit more initial network setup.
[04:18] Tom Briggs: We want the data plane inside our VPC if possible. Direct Connect + TGW seems the most straightforward for low latency. How does Redwood handle DNS and service discovery for private endpoints?
[04:28] Ravi Patel: We can provide private hosted zones (Route53) and a small set of A records for the endpoint. Alternatively, you can point to an ENI or a private IP we allocate in your subnet. Our connector can optionally register an internal SRV record. Some customers prefer the hosted zone approach with cross-account access.
[04:44] Tom Briggs: Cross-account hosted zone delegation is doable. We just need to confirm the zone delegation steps.
[04:48] Maya Chen: We'll send step-by-step docs. Also note, if your VPC has strict egress firewall rules, you may need to open some internal ports for health checks between private nodes; we'll provide the port list.
[05:01] Priya Menon: On the note of firewall, do the private nodes talk outbound to any external telemetry endpoints? Our policy is no telemetry to third-party endpoints without approval.
[05:10] Jordan Lee: Telemetry can be routed to your logging stack. By default we send minimal telemetry to our control plane for health & auto-scaling when using hosted control plane. For fully air-gapped Private, we can disable external telemetry or route through a customer forwarder. We've seen this requirement in healthcare customers.
[05:26] Elena Soto: Good. Now, a few edge cases: we have overlapping CIDRs in some dev VPCs that we can't change quickly. How strict is the non-overlap requirement for peering or private endpoints?
[05:38] Ravi Patel: For VPC peering you need non-overlapping CIDRs. For Transit Gateway attachments there's more flexibility but routing still requires unique prefixes for correct propagation. For private endpoints that create ENIs inside a subnet, overlapping shouldn't be an issue as long as you allocate a dedicated subnet with non-overlapping addresses for the connector. If you can't change existing ranges, the endpoint-in-our-subnet model might be easier.
[06:00] Tom Briggs: So we could host the connector in a dedicated 'redwood-connector' subnet with a small CIDR like /28?
[06:07] Jordan Lee: Exactly. That approach isolates address space and keeps routing straightforward.
[06:11] Priya Menon: Let's talk SLAs — downtime tolerance is low. We need 99.95 for inference times that our product depends on. Does Redwood provide SLA for Private deployments?
[06:21] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we have SLA options in enterprise contracts. For Private, SLA depends on deployment topology — if Redwood manages the nodes we can offer SLA; for customer-managed on-prem it's a collaborative SLA with assumptions. We'll capture the SLOs and failure modes in the runbook we send.
[06:36] Elena Soto: Another requirement — audit trail for every inference request, including request metadata, model version, and output hash. Can that be ingested into our SIEM?
[06:46] Jordan Lee: Yes, we support structured event export. We can log token counts, model id, version, prompt hash and push to CloudWatch/Stackdriver or to S3 with lifecycle policies, which you can then pick up into the SIEM. We do need to be careful about storing raw prompts if they include PHI; many customers prefer prompt redaction in logs.
[07:04] Priya Menon: We'll want prompt redaction and also the ability to run integrity checks on models (image checksums / model hash) to ensure no drift.
[07:12] Ravi Patel: We record model artifacts hash as part of deployment metadata; that's in the control-plane audit. For Private, if you run the control plane in your account, you own that metadata chain.
[07:22] Elena Soto: Good. On billing and metering — we need token-level billing exported to our billing system and preferably a way to cap spend per environment. Can Redwood export token logs to a billing bucket?
[07:34] Maya Chen: Yes, we can push detailed usage logs to S3 with per-route breakdowns. You can also configure quotas and alerts in the console.
[07:42] Carlos Ruiz: One more — latency. When we tested a hosted trial, p95 latency varied quite a bit. We need consistent sub-150ms for small prompts. How would Private affect that?
[07:51] Ravi Patel: Putting inference workers into your region and inside your VPC should reduce network hop variability — most customers see p95 drops by 20-40% compared to public hosted. Batching config and KV cache also influence experienced latency. We can run a small perf test: 1000 requests across your sample prompts from your subnet to a private endpoint and return metrics.
[08:12] Tom Briggs: That'd be helpful. We can provide synthetic prompts and a staging CIDR.
[08:17] Maya Chen: Great, action on that.
[08:19] Elena Soto: Any regulatory showstoppers — like do models ever call out to a central redis or third-party services that would move PHI?
[08:27] Jordan Lee: No, model execution is self-contained. We do use internal caches for KV but those can be provisioned in-customer VPC or be ephemeral and encrypted. We'll include details.
[08:37] Priya Menon: About encryption at rest — do you support customer-managed keys for model caches and for S3 exports?
[08:45] Ravi Patel: Yes. CMKs for S3 and encrypted EBS volumes for workers. For in-memory caches, we use encrypted pages and optional mlock settings; for extremely sensitive workloads we recommend on-prem Private deployment.
[09:00] Carlos Ruiz: Let's surface a quick network checklist so we know what to gather: CIDRs, TGW topology, NAT pools, security group egress rules, DNS delegation preference, SAML IdP metadata.
[09:12] Maya Chen: I'll include that in the follow-up email.
[09:15] Tom Briggs: One more question — how does Redwood handle model updates? If we pin a version, can we opt into security patches but not model architecture changes?
[09:25] Jordan Lee: We support pinned versions and can do canary rollouts. For Dedicated/Private we can push security patches without changing model behavior; major model upgrades are opt-in. We'll document the release process and rollback steps.
[09:38] Elena Soto: Ok, this has been useful. I want to be explicit: next steps for us internally are to get legal and compliance comfortable. Priya, Tom and I will review the security pack; Tom will provide networking artifacts. After that we want a short live test and then a demo of Dedicated vs Private console.
[09:54] Maya Chen: Perfect. To recap our next steps — we'll share SOC2 and ISO docs, network step-by-step for private endpoint & Route53 delegation, and a perf test plan. Ravi will own the perf harness. We'll aim for the demo the following week.
[10:08] Elena Soto: Sounds good. Thanks, team.
[10:11] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

[10:20] (end recording)
